Monte Carlo Sensitivity Analysis for the Budget Constrained Procedure

Source: R/sensitivity_budget.R
seq_budget_sensitivity.Rd

Runs the budget constrained sequential procedure of Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025) from pilot to stopping G times, for population means, standard deviations, costs, and a budget that the user supplies, and summarizes what the procedure delivers: how the budget is spent, how close the final sample sizes and the variance of the contrast estimator come to the optimal allocation of seq_budget_optimal, the coverage of the confidence interval, and, for a given margin, how often the noninferiority test rejects. Use it before a study to see what a budget buys.

Usage

seq_budget_sensitivity(
  true_means,
  true_sds,
  contrast_weights,
  cost_per_group,
  budget,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  distribution = c("normal", "skewed"),
  margin = NULL,
  alpha_level = 0.05,
  G = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  m_0 = 5,
  procedure = c("reallocate", "first_passage")
)

Arguments

true_means

Numeric vector of length K (at least 2): the population means. In a group with a nonzero weight the mean must be less than 1e6 standard deviations (true_sds) from zero. The package treats scores that agree to ten significant digits as showing no variation, and beside a larger mean the simulated studies would begin to depend on where the scores are located. Subtracting a common constant from the means leaves a contrast whose weights sum to zero unchanged.

true_sds

Numeric vector of length K: the population standard deviations, each positive.

contrast_weights

Numeric vector of length K giving the contrast coefficients, not all zero.

cost_per_group

Numeric vector of length K giving the cost of one observation from each population, each positive. The four vector arguments are matched by position; if more than one is named, the names must be the same and in the same order.

budget

The total budget, pilot included: a single positive number. The pilot, which costs m_0 * sum(cost_per_group), must not cost more than the budget, and the budget must not pay for more than one million observations in the cheapest group (see Details).

conf_level

The confidence level of the two-sided interval whose coverage is reported (default 0.95).

distribution

The shape of the populations: "normal" (default) or "skewed"; an unambiguous abbreviation is accepted.

margin

Optional noninferiority margin: the size of the margin, a single positive number, as in decide_seq_budget_noninferiority. When supplied, the rejection rate of that test at this margin is reported. It is the power of the test when the true contrast is above -margin and its Type I error rate when the true contrast is at or below -margin.

alpha_level

The one-sided level of the noninferiority test: a single number strictly between 0 and 0.5 (default 0.05, the default of the decision functions). It is used only when margin is supplied, but is checked either way.

G

Number of Monte Carlo replications: a whole number of at least 2 (default 1000).

seed

Optional whole number that set.seed() accepts. When supplied the replications are reproducible and the random number generator state of the session is restored on exit; NULL (default) uses the current state.

m_0

Pilot sample size per population: a whole number of at least 2 (default 5, as in seq_budget_pilot).

procedure

Which reading of the procedure to run (an unambiguous abbreviation is accepted). "reallocate" (default) is the package's: every group is judged on the current data at each check and the next observation goes to the group furthest below its estimated optimal size. The other choice, "first_passage", follows the article's rule: a group is closed for good the first time it meets its criterion, and the open groups are visited in rounds (closed in seq_budget with order = "rounds" in seq_budget_next).

Value

An object of class c("smsd_sensitivity", "data.frame"): a data frame with columns term and value, one row per quantity, that prints in fixed notation (see smsd_sensitivity_methods) and can otherwise be used as any data frame. With K populations the rows are, in order:

true_contrast

the population contrast, sum(contrast_weights * true_means).

budget, conf_level, replications

the inputs.

coverage

the proportion (0 to 1) of replications whose interval contains the true contrast.

mean_total_cost, sd_total_cost

the mean and standard deviation of the final total cost.

pct_within_budget

the percentage (0 to 100) of replications whose final cost is no more than the budget.

pct_rule_met

the percentage (0 to 100) of replications that ended with every group having met its criterion; the others ended because the budget could not pay for another needed observation.

mean_n_1, ..., mean_n_K

the mean final sample size of each group.

optimal_n_1, ..., optimal_n_K

for comparison, the optimal sample sizes for the true standard deviations, as seq_budget_optimal returns them.

mean_estimated_variance

the mean over replications of the estimated variance of the contrast estimator at stopping (the variance row of the final check).

mean_true_variance

the mean over replications of the true variance of the contrast estimator at the final sample sizes, sum(contrast_weights^2 * true_sds^2 / n). It is never below optimal_variance; the excess is the price of not knowing the standard deviations in advance.

empirical_variance

the mean squared deviation of the contrast estimate from the true contrast over replications: the variance the procedure actually delivered. It has more Monte Carlo error than the two rows above.

optimal_variance

the smallest variance the budget allows with known standard deviations, \(V_o\).

margin, alpha_level

the inputs of the noninferiority test (NA when no margin was supplied).

noninferiority_rejection_rate

the proportion (0 to 1) of replications in which inferiority was rejected (NA when no margin was supplied).

Details

Each replication draws m_0 observations per population, then adds one observation at a time to the group that seq_budget_next names, re-evaluating seq_budget after each, until no group that still needs an observation can be paid for. The total cost can therefore never pass the budget; pct_within_budget reports this and is 100 by construction.

Observations are generated as true_means[i] + true_sds[i] * Z, where \(Z\) is standard normal (distribution = "normal") or a standardized right skewed chi square variable with 3 degrees of freedom ("skewed"; skewness about 1.63).

The interval and the test are asymptotic, and the size of the shortfall for a design of interest is what this function reports. As a guide, in runs of 10,000 replications (standard error about 0.002) over five designs with a pilot of 10 and about 15 to 120 observations per group, coverage of the 95 percent interval was 0.936 to 0.949 for normal populations and 0.925 to 0.941 for skewed ones, and the rejection rate of the noninferiority test at the margin (nominal 0.05) was 0.050 to 0.061 for normal populations and 0.040 to 0.085 for skewed ones. The default pilot of 5 does a little worse than that when the populations are skewed and the budget is small, and a pilot of 2 does much worse; seq_budget_pilot has the figures, and m_0 lets the comparison be made for the design at hand.

procedure = "first_passage" is the package's reading of the article's sequence, and differs from it in three details that the help page of seq_budget_next sets out; the main one is that every open group is judged after each observation, where the article judges a population only after an observation drawn from it.

Each step of a replication recomputes the standard deviation of the group that received the observation, so the time for one replication grows faster than the number of observations the budget buys: on one core of the computer used to check the package, the default G = 1000 took about 6 seconds when a study ended with about 200 observations in all, about 2 minutes with about 3,200, and about 11 minutes with about 12,800. For a budget that buys thousands of observations, start with a small G. A budget that pays for more than one million observations in the cheapest group (budget / min(cost_per_group)) is refused before anything is simulated: at that limit, with costs of 38, 15, and 10, a study ended with about 415,000 observations and one replication took more than two minutes.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J. (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570

See also

seq_budget, seq_budget_next, seq_budget_optimal, decide_seq_budget_noninferiority. In DMAR, ss_seq_c_sensitivity is the corresponding study for the sequential fixed-width interval for a contrast.

Other seq_budget: decide_seq_budget, seq_budget(), seq_budget_next(), seq_budget_optimal(), seq_budget_pilot()

Examples

# A new training format (group 1) against the average of two existing
# ones, with unequal costs and a budget of 1,500. G = 100 keeps the
# example quick; a reported analysis deserves the default G = 1000 or
# more.
seq_budget_sensitivity(
  true_means = c(50, 50, 50),
  true_sds = c(9, 6, 6),
  contrast_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),
  cost_per_group = c(38, 15, 10),
  budget = 1500,
  margin = 5,
  G = 100,
  seed = 113,
  m_0 = 10
)
#> term                           value
#> true_contrast                  0
#> budget                         1500
#> conf_level                     0.95
#> replications                   100
#> coverage                       0.92
#> mean_total_cost                1490.74
#> sd_total_cost                  8.192902
#> pct_within_budget              100
#> pct_rule_met                   0
#> mean_n_1                       28.28
#> mean_n_2                       15.22
#> mean_n_3                       18.78
#> optimal_n_1                    28.59535
#> optimal_n_2                    15.17121
#> optimal_n_3                    18.58086
#> mean_estimated_variance        3.707542
#> mean_true_variance             3.989052
#> empirical_variance             4.883586
#> optimal_variance               3.910227
#> margin                         5
#> alpha_level                    0.05
#> noninferiority_rejection_rate  0.75
